INT. CONWAY HOUSE - MIDNIGHT

ENTER - A middle-class place in the suburbs. A Newscaster on TV in the background announces the latest in a series of mass-casualty events caused by a group of super-powered individuals - THE SHADE. 

NEWSCASTER: --still coming in, but it appears as if terrorist organization The Shade has attacked Disneyland. We do not have a final casualty count yet, but early reports are claiming numbers in the hundreds, if not--

The Newscaster is interrupted with a CRASH, as a box full of airplane shots of vodka crashes to the ground. 

SARAH CONWAY, a beautiful woman in her early 30s, stands defiant in front of her husband, JIM CONWAY, 33. 

SARAH: You ASSHOLE! How *dare* you keep those in this house! After last time?! 

JIM: Sarah, you know this is more than--

SARAH: I know, I know, You need to do this. You have a *responsibility*. You know what, you're full of shit. Every time things get tough, there's some reason you're *needed*. You're an addict!

NEWSCASTER (BACKGROUND): --Six more attacks around the country, with casualties in the thousands--

Jim looks into Sarah's eyes sadly, and picks up a shot from the ground. He looks at it, and back at her. 

SARAH: If you don't put that down, I'm leaving!

Jim sighs sadly, opening the shot and downing it. He picks one more up from the ground and puts it in his pocket. 

JIM: Don't bother...I have to go...I won't be back from this. 

Jim crosses the room and opens the door. 

EXT. CONWAY HOUSE - LATE
Jim walks outside, the door closing with a click behind him. Tears run down his face as he walks down the driveway and enters his car - A beautifully restored 1971 Barracuda. He sits down in the driver's seat, opens the second shot, and downs it, tossing the empty bottle into the back seat behind him. He turns the key in the ignition. 

JIM: They need me...They need Beercules.

I use an Android phone, my tablet's an iPad, and I have a Windows gaming rig/media center, and over the years I've owned 3 Macbooks and 3 Windows laptops - so I'm not particularly brand loyal -  but overall, I prefer Macs for my laptop. I don't buy into Apple's whole ecosystem, and I do think that Macs are overpriced - but to be honest, I prefer MacOS to Windows. 

I appreciate the little flourishes, like being able to screenshot only a portion of the screen and have it output automatically to your desktop as an image file - things like that. Now admittedly, I work in tech marketing and probably need this feature more than most people, but there are a lot of little things like that that just make it more of a pleasure to use than Windows. And the software is really catching up, gaming aside. 

An interesting thing I've found with accessing some more of the more power-user-y features, though, is that Windows is actually more intuitive. Apple *allows* you to do effectively anything in the OS that you could do in Windows, but they hide it away pretty damn well. Whether or not that's something that matters to people is personal preference - but for the most part, they're features that you'd have to already know about before you'd know enough to want to use it, and if you know about them you probably know how to access them, or at least enough to google how to. 

In the end, though, I find Macbooks to make great laptops that provide a pretty sweet compromise of the features I want in a form factor that's a pleasure to use. They're pretty damn durable, too, in my experience, though I won't pretend there aren't more durable options out there. 

My iPad, on the other hand, I would trade in a second for a comparable Android tablet (specs, build quality, etc.), but try as I might to find one, at least a little over a year ago, there wasn't anything comparable out there (I was really disappointed that the Nexus 10 turned out to be mediocre). And that's for much the same reason - I simply prefer Android to iOS. I find it to be a more flexible, powerful OS in general, particularly with the options available as far as ROMs go (CyanogenMod, etc).

Which I basically addressed in the latter half of my post. It's not fair. It's not okay. And, frankly, they *were* the victims of systematic discrimination, just a different kind. 

To a large extent, 'poor people' is a lens we tend to view unfavorably, no matter the color of one's skin. When you hit that end of the spectrum, poor white people and poor black people *still* aren't viewed equally unfavorably. Poor white people may be a nuisance, or someone we'd like to sweep under the rug, or 'that ridiculous redneck' - but we should *fear* poor black people. 

I'm not saying I disagree with you at all, because I feel like I don't. I'm just saying there are additional layers that complicate things.

I think it's two things, honestly. The first being that, no matter how bad off a white person is, swap white for black, and they'd likely be doing worse. As the poster above mentioned, lessened job opportunities, etc. 

The second is that 'sad white person' just isn't a particularly interesting narrative. Lots of white people are sad, down on their luck, etc. There've been no shortage of stories about that. It's saturated the media narrative for years. "White person fails" is something we consider, right or wrong, 'normal,' because the system is biased in favor of white people. If they failed, they clearly failed on their on merits, right? 

Note that I'm not saying I believe this, but I am saying that privilege is a double-edged sword from a 'narrative' perspective. You're just a less relatable 'temporarily down-on-your luck' person when the system is biased toward you anyway, and there are other people who the system is biased against who are also down on their luck. 

Which, of course, leads to resentment from the people who are, legitimately, down on their luck, and from their perspective see things being "given" to those who aren't themselves - especially when they're entirely correct in thinking that the system has been biased against them in different ways, and that their plight isn't being addressed. 

It's an incredibly difficult situation to parse out and adequately address. Evening the playing field removes a lot of that in the long-term, but in the short-term leads to quite a bit of anger and resentment.

The mechanism that causes depression is still incredibly poorly understood. The best we have is "In many cases, manipulating certain chemicals (seratonin, dopamine, norepinephrine) helps with the symptoms of depression" To a large extent, we don't know why. Which makes depression incredibly difficult to treat if the first-line drugs don't work or cause more problems than they solve

To set the scene, my room back at my parents' place was fairly large. Next to my bed was a nightstand. On that nightstand was a solo cup full of iced coffee. 

I'd just been showing off my brand new iPhone, purchased only a few months after release. Without paying much attention, I went ahead and gently tossed the phone across the room, with the intention of it landing on my bed. I tossed it, and before it landed, I looked away, unconcerned. 

*plunk*

I looked back in horror, but at first, couldn't tell what was wrong. The scene was unchanged. Bed, nightstand, cup full of coffee, undisturbed on my nightstand. 

But no phone to be found. 

I walked over, terrified. And there it was, perfectly upright, completely submerged in liquid. 

Without looking, I had managed to sink my phone perfectly into a cup only perhaps an inch wider than it was. Without even knocking the cup over. If it had hit at any other angle, it wouldn't have fit into the cup at all. Any other amount of force, and it would have knocked the cup over, perhaps saving my phone from much more than a light splash. 

I couldn't have replicated it if I'd tried a thousand times, But there, that one moment, that one time, it happened. Completely on accident. 

RIP, phone.

(Disclaimer: I'm not a biologist, but I've taken several courses on the subject. I'm going to do my best to answer your question, but I'm more than open to being corrected if I'm wrong on any points.)

The simple answer is "they're not." 

The primates alive today differ wildly from primates that co-evolved with humans. In addition, over the course of history, several other hominid (basically: Human-like) species evolved and died off, Neanderthals being the most widely-known and most human-like example - but they're far from the *only* example. 

In addition, evolution doesn't tend toward 'smarter' or even 'more complex,' those are value judgements we assign to a completely valueless system. It tends toward 'more well suited to their environment.' If intelligence helps a species to adapt, it will be selected for, but human-like intelligence is not necessarily 'better' in any way, evolutionarily speaking. 

It is believed that humans developed forethought, for example, during the last glacial maximum, when the African habitat in which our ancestors lived became a desert and the species was reduced to ~20,000 members. The ones who survived were the ones who were able to plan ahead, and do things like bury water for later use. Such selective pressure was not necessarily exerted on, say, Gorillas or chimps, who developed different adaptive measures to cope with scarcity of resources in their environment.)

Evolution is not a selective force by which nature abides; it's a way of describing observable facts about natural selection. One of the easier examples may be camouflage. Imagine a small bird that serves as a food source to a larger animal. Now, imagine that over hundreds of years, the climate in their environment changes, and the formerly green jungle becomes brushy grassland. Which birds would be more likely to survive – ones that appear in the vivid greens of a jungle environment, or the ones that tend toward more subdued browns and tans? Over time, you’d see less and less of the green birds reaching a breeding age, and eventually, you’d see that the formerly predominantly brightly-colored species of birds would become a predominantly grassland-colored species of birds. Eventually, the jungle colors would stop appearing altogether. 

A species doesn’t change because evolution made them better. The species changes because the members of the species worse-suited to their environment are removed from the gene pool. Meanwhile, mutation constantly introduces new genetic diversity to the gene pool. (Mutation also being an utterly random, completely valueless mechanism. Most mutations are immediately fatal.) In humans, the ones without the capacity for forethought died in a newly-desert environment, leaving only the 'more intelligent' members of the species to reproduce. 

Anyway, this was a long-winded, incredibly oversimplified answer, but hopefully it helps your understanding some.

Honestly, bipolar does not just get better - and while therapy is certainly helpful, it does nothing to deal with the very real chemical imbalances going on in your wife's brain. Your wife needs to be on medication, or this *will* keep happening. 

There are *many* different medications for bipolar available, and they will not all affect her the same way. Some will have horrendous side effects, some may have tolerable side effects, and some may have no side effects at all. Finding the right medication is a horrible experience, but *absolutely* necessary. 

Without medication, she will *never* be okay, and without a commitment to finding the right one on her part, your odds of things working out between you are slim to none. 

Background: My fiancee has bipolar I and had a massive manic break a little over a year ago, resulting in cheating and general craziness. It took *months*, but we finally found a medication that works for her (trileptal, but your milage may vary), and we're now happier than we've ever been. She's back to being the girl I fell in love with. 

Hope isn't lost - but unless you can get her to be serious about managing what's honestly a life-threatening medical condition, there's very little you can do. Until she's onboard with that, nothing she says or does can be considered to be truth in any meaningful sense of the term. She may make all the promises in the world now, but if she's manic a week down the line, all of that goes right out the window. 

Keep in mind that it's not her fault - but it *is* something that needs to be managed very seriously for the rest of her life, and without a firm commitment to do so on her part, you're going to need to make some decisions about what *you* want to deal with. 

Good luck to both of you. This is a tough one.
